claims.text: Single-phase BCC refractory high-entropy alloys can retain unusually high yield strength at elevated temperatures.
Edge dislocations can control high-temperature strength and strength retention in BCC RHEAs.
The thermoelastic stability of single-phase RHEAs is primarily caused by edge-dislocation-mediated plasticity.
Intrinsic lattice distortion is a primary cause of edge-dislocation-mediated high-temperature plasticity.
Temperature-induced elastic anisotropy contributes causally to the exceptional high-temperature strength and thermoelastic stability.
Increasing lattice distortion by changing the refractory-element mixture favors edge-dislocation motion over screw-dislocation activation.
Favoring edge-dislocation motion enhances yield-strength retention at high temperature.
Favoring edge-dislocation motion reduces thermoelastic softening at high temperature.
NbTaTiVZr and NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 are candidate single-phase BCC random solid solutions with significant inherent lattice distortion.
Compositional variations can be used to amplify or reduce lattice distortion for a controlled high-temperature comparison.
The comparison will cover room temperature through approximately 1200 K under controlled strain rates.
Lattice distortion and elastic anisotropy govern the density and mobility of edge dislocations.
Enhanced lattice distortion lowers the energetic barrier for edge-dislocation motion.
Enhanced lattice distortion simultaneously increases elastic anisotropy.
Conventional BCC elemental metals and dilute alloys generally exhibit screw-dislocation-controlled plastic flow.
More highly distorted RHEAs will retain greater yield strength and show less thermoelastic softening than less distorted RHEAs or conventional BCC alloys.
More highly distorted RHEAs will exhibit a predominantly edge-character dislocation structure at high temperature.
The proposed mechanism is limited to single-phase BCC RHEAs and may fail when phase segregation, phase instability, or impurity-driven softening dominates.
Failure of the high-distortion specimens to show greater strength retention, less elastic softening, and more edge dislocations than the low-distortion controls would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The mechanism says lattice distortion lowers the barrier to edge-dislocation motion, which ordinarily facilitates plastic flow, but then attributes higher yield strength to that lowered barrier without explaining how easier dislocation motion raises the stress required for yielding.
